flashcards.back: It is usually treated as `0`, with no error (so `[[ hello -eq 0 ]]` is true).
True if the variable `x` has been assigned a value (even empty). Write the name, not `$x`.

flashcards.front: Standard usage-message check for a script that needs exactly one argument
flashcards.back:
```bash
if (( $# != 1 )); then
    echo "Usage: script.sh arg" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

flashcards.front: Quiz 2 Q1E: print `not readable` if the file named in `f` is not readable
flashcards.back: `if [[ ! -r $f ]]; then echo "not readable"; fi`

flashcards.front: Validator script (like `testpw.sh`): how do you report EVERY failed rule and still exit with status 2?
flashcards.back: `status=0` at the start; one separate `if` per rule that prints its message with `>&2` and sets `status=2`; `exit $status` at the end.

flashcards.front: `while` vs `until`?
flashcards.back: `while` loops while the test command succeeds (status 0); `until` loops while it fails (stops when it succeeds).

flashcards.front: Write a while loop that prints 1 to 5.
flashcards.back: `i=1; while (( i <= 5 )); do echo $i; (( i++ )); done`

flashcards.front: Syntax of a C-style for loop counting i from 0 to n-1.
flashcards.back: `for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do ... done`

flashcards.front: Loop over each command line argument.
flashcards.back: `for arg in "$@"; do ... done`

flashcards.front: Why must `$@` be quoted in `for arg in "$@"`?
flashcards.back: Unquoted, each argument is word-split, so `"a b"` becomes two iterations (see `bad_for_each_arg.sh`).

flashcards.front: What does `shift` do?
flashcards.back: Moves the positional parameters left by one (`$2` becomes `$1`, ...), drops the old `$1`, and decreases `$#` by 1.

flashcards.front: Process arguments with `while` and `shift`.
flashcards.back: `while (( $# > 0 )); do echo "$1"; shift; done`

flashcards.front: `for f in *.pdf` when no `.pdf` files exist?
flashcards.back: The body runs once with `f` set to the literal text `*.pdf`.

flashcards.front: Guard a glob loop against the no-match case.
flashcards.back: First line of the body: `[[ -e $f ]] || continue` (or `shopt -s nullglob` before the loop).

flashcards.front: Loop over the subdirectories of the current directory.
flashcards.back: `for d in */; do ... done` (each `d` ends with `/`, e.g. `stu1/`)

flashcards.front: Loop over the characters of string `s`.
`break` vs `continue`?
flashcards.back: `break` exits the loop; `continue` skips to the next iteration. `break 2` / `continue 2` act on an outer loop.

flashcards.front: Read the file named in `$file` one line at a time.
flashcards.back: `while read -r line; do ...; done < "$file"`

flashcards.front: Why `-r` in `read -r`?
flashcards.back: So backslashes in the input are kept as ordinary characters.

flashcards.front: Split comma-separated lines into fields while reading.
flashcards.back: `while IFS="," read -r a b c; do ...; done < "$file"`

flashcards.front: Why is `for i in $(seq 1 10)` discouraged in the course?
flashcards.back: `seq 1 10` is a separate program that prints 1 to 10; the shell must start a new process just to count. A C-style `for (( i = 1; i <= 10; i++ ))` loop does it in the shell.

flashcards.front: Write an infinite loop two ways.
flashcards.back: `while true; do ... done` or `until false; do ... done` (leave it with `break`, or Ctrl + C).

flashcards.front: What does `(( count-- ))` do?
flashcards.back: Subtracts 1 from `count` (same as `count=$(( count - 1 ))`).

flashcards.front: `str="a  b c"; for w in $str; do ...` runs how many times?
flashcards.back: 3 times (`a`, `b`, `c`): the unquoted variable is word split.

flashcards.front: Loop over the numbers 1 to 10 with brace expansion.
flashcards.back: `for i in {1..10}; do ... done`

flashcards.front: Loop over each element of array `arr` (elements may contain spaces).
flashcards.back: `for x in "${arr[@]}"; do ... done`

flashcards.front: Loop over the indexes in use in array `arr` (even if it is sparse).
flashcards.back: `for i in "${!arr[@]}"; do echo "${arr[i]}"; done`

flashcards.front: Visit array `arr` from its last element to its first.
flashcards.back: `for (( i = ${#arr[@]} - 1; i >= 0; i-- )); do echo "${arr[i]}"; done`

flashcards.front: How many times does `for x in "${arr[*]}"` run when `arr=(a b c)`?
flashcards.back: Once: `"${arr[*]}"` is one word, `a b c`.

flashcards.front: Inside `(( ))`, how do you write element `i` of `arr`?
flashcards.back: `arr[i]` (no `$`, no braces), e.g. `(( total += arr[i] ))`. Outside `(( ))` write `${arr[i]}`.

flashcards.front: When does `while read -r line; do ... done < "$file"` stop?
flashcards.back: When `read` fails: at the end of the file (no more complete lines).

flashcards.front: `IFS="," read -r a b` on the line `x,y,z`: what are `a` and `b`?
flashcards.back: `a` is `x`; `b` is `y,z` (the last variable gets the rest of the line).

flashcards.front: Nested loops: the outer loop makes 3 passes, the inner loop 4 per pass. How many times does the inner body run?
flashcards.back: 12 (the inner loop runs completely for each outer pass).

flashcards.front: In `[[ -e $f ]] || continue`, what does `||` do?
flashcards.back: Runs `continue` only if the test fails, i.e. when `$f` does not exist (the literal unmatched glob).

flashcards.front: In nested loops, which loop does a plain `break` leave?
flashcards.back: Only the innermost loop it is in; the outer loop goes on. `break 2` leaves both.

flashcards.front: Course syntax to define a function `greet`.
flashcards.back: `greet() {` newline, commands, newline `}`

flashcards.front: What are the brace rules for a function body?
flashcards.back: A space or newline after `{`; the `}` must start a new command (its own line, or after `;`).

flashcards.front: What happens if you call a function before its definition in a script?
flashcards.back: `command not found`: the definition has not run yet.

flashcards.front: Inside a function, what are `$1` and `$#`?
flashcards.back: The function's own first argument and its number of arguments (the script's are hidden until it returns).

flashcards.front: Call function `f` with all of the script's arguments.
What is a function's exit status if it has no `return`?
flashcards.back: The exit status of the last command it ran.

flashcards.front: What range can `return n` produce?
flashcards.back: 0-255 (lowest 8 bits of n); `return 256` gives 0.

flashcards.front: `return` vs `exit` inside a function?
flashcards.back: `return` ends the function; `exit` ends the whole script.

flashcards.front: Two ways to get a value out of a Bash function.
flashcards.back: 1. `echo` it and capture with `var=$(f args)`. 2. Assign a non-local (global) variable that the caller reads.

flashcards.front: What is dynamic scoping?
flashcards.back: A function sees the variables of whoever called it (and their callers); variables it sets are visible to the caller afterwards unless `local`.

flashcards.front: What does `local x=5` do?
flashcards.back: Creates `x` only for this function call (and functions it calls), leaving any caller's `x` untouched.

flashcards.front: Load the functions in `funcs.sh` into the current shell.
flashcards.back: `source ./funcs.sh` (or `. ./funcs.sh`)

flashcards.front: Use function `is_int` as a condition.
flashcards.back: `if is_int "$1"; then ... fi` (true when it returns 0)

flashcards.front: After `i=$(indexof z abc)`, what is `$?`?
flashcards.back: The exit status of `indexof` (1 if it returned 1): an assignment with `$( )` has the status of the command inside.
Both are legal Bash. The `function` form is not portable; the course writes `f() { ... }`.

flashcards.front: `f` sets `y=5` and prints `hi`. After `x=$(f)`, what are `x` and `y`?
flashcards.back: `x` is `hi`; `y` is unchanged (unset), because `$( )` ran `f` in a subshell.

flashcards.front: In selection sort, what does `minidx j` find?
flashcards.back: The index of the smallest element of `arr` from index `j` to the end.

flashcards.front: Swap `arr[j]` and `arr[idx]`.
flashcards.back: `tmp=${arr[j]}`, then `arr[j]=${arr[idx]}`, then `arr[idx]=$tmp`.

flashcards.front: Why quote the right side in `[[ ${s:i:1} == "${s:j:1}" ]]`?
flashcards.back: Unquoted, the right side of `==` is a glob pattern, so a `*` or `?` character would match anything. Quoted, it is compared literally.

flashcards.front: Should a function in a file meant for `source` end with `exit 1` on failure?
flashcards.back: No: use `return 1`. `exit` would end the shell that sourced the file (it can close your terminal).

quiz.explain: Integer division drops the fraction; `%` is the remainder; `**` is power.

quiz.code:
x=5
x=$x+1
echo $x
x=5
x=$(( x + 1 ))
echo $x
quiz.explain: A plain assignment just builds a string. Only `$(( ))` (or `(( ))`) does arithmetic.

quiz.code:
x=abc; y=5
(( z = x + y ))
echo $z
(( z++ ))
(( z *= 2 ))
echo $z
quiz.explain: A non-numeric value counts as 0, so `z` is 5; then 6; then 12.
`(( ))` succeeds (status 0) when the value is non-zero and fails (status 1) when it is 0.
Normal precedence (`*` before `+`). `10 / 3` is 3, so `10 / 3 * 3` is 9: the fraction is lost before multiplying.

quiz.q: Which line prints a random integer from 1 to 10 inclusive?
quiz.explain: `RANDOM % 10` is 0 to 9, plus 1 gives 1 to 10. `% 11` gives 0 to 10. The last has no arithmetic expansion, so it prints a number followed by the literal text `% 10 + 1`.

quiz.q: Write the start of a script that requires **at least** 2 arguments: if fewer are given it prints `need 2 args` to standard error and exits with status 1.
quiz.answer:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

if (( $# < 2 )); then
    echo "need 2 args" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```
quiz.explain: Also correct: `[[ $# -lt 2 ]]` (from the conditional statements topic). `(( $# < 2 ))` compares numbers.

quiz.q: Which line creates an array `arr` holding the three values 1, 2 and 3?
quiz.explain: Elements go in parentheses separated by spaces. Commas would become part of the elements (`1,`), square brackets do not make an array, and spaces around `=` make Bash run `arr` as a command.
`${#arr[@]}` is the number of elements (3). Indexes start at 0, so index 1 is the second element, 20.

quiz.code:
arr=(red green blue)
echo $arr
echo $arr[2]
quiz.explain: `$arr` alone means element 0. In `$arr[2]` only `$arr` is expanded; `[2]` is plain text. You need `${arr[2]}` to get `blue`.

quiz.code:
arr=([3]=c [7]=g)
arr+=(h)
echo "${!arr[@]}"
echo "${#arr[@]}"
quiz.explain: The array is sparse: indexes 3 and 7. Appending puts `h` after the largest index, at 8. There are 3 elements, even though the largest index is 8.

Each word an expansion produces becomes one element of the new array. Quoted `@`: one word per element (2). Quoted `*`: one single word (1), which is `a dog a cat`. Unquoted: word splitting gives 4 words.

quiz.q: The array `files` holds filenames, some containing spaces. Which command removes exactly those files, passing each filename to `rm` as one argument?
quiz.explain: `"${files[@]}"` expands to one quoted word per element. Unquoted `@` splits names at spaces; quoted `*` gives one big word (one name that does not exist); `"$files"` is only element 0.

quiz.code:
arr=(a b)
arr+=c
arr+=(d)
echo "${arr[@]}"
echo "${#arr[@]}"
quiz.explain: `arr+=c` without parentheses appends the text `c` to element 0, making `ac`. `arr+=(d)` adds a new element. So 3 elements: `ac`, `b`, `d`.

quiz.q: The script `count.sh` is run as `./count.sh one "two three" four`. What does it print?
quiz.code:
#!/bin/bash
arr=("$@")
echo "${#arr[@]}"
echo "${arr[1]}"
echo "${arr[2]}"
quiz.explain: `arr=("$@")` makes one element per argument, keeping `two three` whole. So there are 3 elements; index 1 is `two three` and index 2 is `four`.

quiz.q: The file `colors.txt` contains three lines: `red`, `light green`, `blue`. What does this print?
quiz.code:
mapfile -t c < colors.txt
echo "${#c[@]}"
echo "${c[1]}"
quiz.explain: `mapfile -t` stores one line per element (spaces inside a line are kept) and strips the newlines. 3 lines give 3 elements; index 1 is the second line.

quiz.q: Write the Bash lines that swap the elements at indexes `i` and `j` of the array `arr`.
quiz.explain: You need a temporary variable, otherwise the first assignment overwrites a value you still need. `${arr[$i]}` is equally fine.

quiz.code:
yr=1900
if (( yr % 400 == 0 || (yr % 4 == 0 && yr % 100 != 0) )); then
    echo "$yr is a leap year"
else
    echo "$yr is not a leap year"
fi
quiz.explain: 1900 % 400 is 300, so the left side is false. 1900 is divisible by 4 but also by 100, so the parenthesised part is false too.

quiz.q: The file `nosuch` does not exist. In `[[ -e nosuch && -r nosuch ]]`, what happens?
options: Both tests run and the result is false
Only `-e` runs; the result is false (short-circuit)
Bash prints an error because the file is missing
Only `-r` runs because `&&` is evaluated right to left
quiz.explain: `&&` stops as soon as the left side is false: the whole expression must be false, so `-r` is never evaluated. No error is printed; file tests on missing files are simply false.

quiz.code:
s=""
if [[ ! -z $s || -n $s ]]; then echo yes; else echo no; fi
quiz.explain: `s` is empty, so `-z $s` is true and `! -z $s` is false; `-n $s` is false. false || false is false.

quiz.q: Which condition is true exactly when the integer `x` is between 3 and 10 (exclusive)?
quiz.explain: Both comparisons must hold, so `&&`, with integer operators. Option A compares strings (`"5" < "10"` is false). Options B and D use `||`, true for every integer.

quiz.code:
if true; then echo "true"; fi
if false; then echo "false"; fi
echo done
quiz.explain: The condition is a command. `true` exits with 0 (true) so its `echo` runs. `false` exits with 1, the condition fails, and there is no `else`, so nothing is printed.

quiz.q: What is wrong with `if [[$x == 5]]; then echo hi; fi`?
options: Nothing; it prints hi if x is 5
There must be a space after `[[` and before `]]`
quiz.explain: `[[` and `]]` must be separate words. With x=5 Bash tries to run a command named `[[5` (`[[5: command not found`). `==` compares strings, which works for `5`; quoting is optional inside `[[ ]]`.

quiz.code: if [[ 100 < 2 ]]; then echo "100 comes first"; else echo "2 comes first"; fi
quiz.explain: Inside `[[ ]]`, `<` compares strings lexicographically: `1` comes before `2`, so "100" < "2" is true. Use `-lt` or `(( ))` for numbers.

quiz.code:
x=hello
if [[ $x -eq 0 ]]; then echo zero; else echo "not zero"; fi
quiz.explain: In an integer test, a non-integer word like `hello` is treated as 0 (no error), so `0 -eq 0` is true.

quiz.code:
str="avocado"
if [[ $str == a* ]]; then echo "pattern match"; else echo "no pattern match"; fi
if [[ $str == "a*" ]]; then echo "equal to a*"; else echo "not equal to a*"; fi
quiz.answer:
pattern match
not equal to a*
quiz.explain: Unquoted `a*` on the right of `==` is a glob pattern (starts with a). Quoted `"a*"` is the literal two-character string, which `avocado` is not.

quiz.code:
str="K7L 3N6"
if [[ $str == [A-Z][0-9][A-Z][0-9][A-Z][0-9] ]]; then
    echo "might be a postal code"
else
    echo "not a postal code"
fi
quiz.explain: The pattern describes exactly six characters. The space makes the string seven characters, and the 4th character is a space, not a digit.

quiz.code:
x=7
if (( x > 10 )); then
    echo big
elif (( x > 5 )); then
    echo medium
else
    echo small
fi
quiz.explain: `7 > 10` is false, so Bash tries the `elif`: `7 > 5` is true, so it prints `medium` and skips the `else`. Inside `(( ))`, `>` is a numeric comparison.

quiz.q: `notes` is a directory and `empty.txt` is an empty regular file. Which test is **false**?
quiz.explain: `-s` needs size greater than zero, and `empty.txt` is empty. `-e` is true for any existing file (including directories); `-d` is true for the directory.

quiz.q: Suppose the variable `f` stores the name of a file. Write an `if` statement that prints `not writable` to standard output if the file is not writable.
quiz.explain: Same shape as Quiz 2 Q1E with `-w` instead of `-r`. Also accepted: the multi-line form, or `[[ ! -w "$f" ]]`. Common mistakes: no spaces inside `[[ ]]`, no `;` before `then`, forgetting `fi`.

quiz.q: Which `if` statement correctly tests whether the variable `x` has been assigned a value?
quiz.explain: `-v` takes the variable's **name**. `-v $x` would test a variable named by x's value. `-z x` tests the literal string "x" (never empty). `[[ $x ]]` is false for a variable assigned the empty string.

quiz.q: Write the lines at the start of a script that print `Usage: count.sh file` to standard error and exit with status 1 when the number of command line arguments is not exactly 1.
quiz.answer:
```bash
if (( $# != 1 )); then
    echo "Usage: count.sh file" >&2
    exit 1
fi
```
quiz.explain: `[[ $# -ne 1 ]]` is equally good. Both `>&2` (stderr) and `exit 1` are needed; without `exit` the script would carry on.

quiz.q: `compstr.sh` is the course script below. What does `./compstr.sh tiger poodle` print?
quiz.code:
#!/bin/bash

s1=$1
s2=$2
if [[ $s1 == $s2 ]]; then
    echo 0
elif [[ $s1 < $s2 ]]; then
    echo -1
else
    echo 1
fi

    for (( i = $1 + 1; i < n; i++ )); do
        if (( arr[i] < arr[idx] )); then
            idx=$i
        fi
    done
}

# sort: selection sort of the global array arr
sort() {
    local j tmp
    n=${#arr[@]}
    for (( j = 0; j < n; j++ )); do
        minidx "$j"
        tmp=${arr[j]}
        arr[j]=${arr[idx]}
        arr[idx]=$tmp

**Printing.** `echo "${arr[@]}"` prints all elements separated by single spaces on one line.

# hasdups STR

# (i is its first index, j the index of its next copy) and returns 0;
# prints nothing and returns 1 if STR has no repeated characters
hasdups() {
    local s=$1
    local n=${#s}

    local str=$2
